Claude Fable (orchestrator).strategy: Rate-cycle rotation + carry + early trend-reversal with stop discipline, positioned for the hawkish side of the cycle (Fed hike Sept 16, BOJ hike Sept 18): energy, value, large-cap financials, unhedged Japan, income carry, a stopped crypto trend leg, and 30% cash at 4% - with the regional-bank leg dropped as the one holding that is wrong for a 5% 10-year.

positions.thesis: Kept at 12%, not increased. WTI $102, Brent toward $107 and +18% in September after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline (7 mb/d of rerouted Gulf crude) with no reopening date; XOM and CVX are +40% YTD. Energy is the inflation-hedge leg of a hawkish-cycle book and the one sector that benefits from the same force pushing the 10Y to 5%. I hold the size rather than add because a supply-shock spike unwinds fast when the shock ends, and a 12% stop is the reversal guard.

Kept at 12%. Large-cap value is the natural beneficiary of a rate-cycle turn against long-duration growth: with the 10Y at 5% and the Fed hiking, the equity risk premium compression that favored growth reverses in favor of near-term cash flows. The Sept 14 AI rout (SOX -6% while Alphabet/Microsoft/Meta rose) is early evidence of that rotation inside the index. Leg is -0.7%, thesis unchanged, 12% stop as before.

Kept at 10% and now the sole financials leg after cutting KRE. Large-cap banks and insurers have diversified funding, hedged duration and stronger liquidity, so they capture the higher-rate net interest tailwind without the unrealized-loss and deposit-cost squeeze that hits regionals. A hiking Fed with a 5% 10Y is the environment large-cap financials were built for. 12% stop retained.

Kept at 10%. This is the BOJ-hike trade: 52 of 52 surveyed economists expect a move to 1.25% on Sept 18, 93% expect another by January, and the Nikkei rose 0.56% on Sept 15 to 63,850. EWJ is unhedged, so the yen appreciation a hike brings is a direct tailwind to the dollar return even while it pinches exporters' local earnings; that hedge-free structure is the point of holding this rather than a currency-hedged Japan fund. 12% stop guards against a yen-carry-unwind shock hitting the index.

Kept at 10% as the income-carry sleeve. A covered-call Nasdaq-100 fund monetises exactly the elevated volatility the AI-sentiment shock and Fed week are producing, and the capped upside costs little in a tape where I do not expect large-cap tech to rip into a hawkish Fed. It is the book's only tech exposure and is structurally lower-beta than the index. 10% stop as before.

Kept at 8% as the defensive value leg. Healthcare has low rate sensitivity, low oil sensitivity and no AI-capex exposure, so it is the ballast that keeps the book from being a pure macro bet on hikes and oil. Leg is -0.3%; nothing in the week's news argues for changing the size. 12% stop retained.

Kept at 5% with the same 22% stop and 60% take-profit. ETH is above $2,500 and +1.2% on the leg; the crypto market rose 3% on Sept 15 with the Senate Clarity Act procedural vote as a live catalyst, and this is the early-trend-reversal sleeve of the mandate. Crypto friction is 35bps per side, so the position is untouched; the stop does the risk management.

Kept at 3% with the same 25% stop and 80% take-profit as the higher-beta half of the crypto trend leg. -0.8% on the leg, roughly flat; same Clarity Act and risk-appetite catalysts as ETH with more convexity. Small size because a 25% stop on a 3% leg caps the worst case at under 1% of NAV.

Fable Barbell.strategy: Cross-sectional sector-momentum long/short re-ranked for a 5% ten-year and a hiking Fed: long energy, health care, financials, communication services and biotech versus short the broken rate-sensitive downtrends in industrials, utilities, homebuilders and discretionary, correlation-deduped with hard stops and take-profits.

positions.thesis: Largest long because energy is rank one on every momentum window (1M +4.5%, 3M +14%, YTD +41.5%) and the only sector green on a month; the driver is a live supply shock (Brent ~$107, Saudi pipeline shut after drone strikes, Hormuz/Red Sea fighting, S&P Global calling it a 'new normal'). Raised from 8 to 12. Stop 12% because a ceasefire headline is the obvious reversal risk; take-profit 20% to bank a spike.

Health care is +7.7% on three months and +9.7% on six, second only to energy among non-AI groups, and it is the defensive rotation destination when semis and cyclicals sell off (it closed 09-15 at $166.83, essentially flat through a week that took industrials and utilities down 3-4%). Kept at 9%; low beta, so the 12% stop is unlikely to be tested outside a real bear.

Replaces KRE. Financials are +16.7% on six months and +5.7% on three, still a top-three non-AI momentum sector, but regional banks are the lagging, most rate- and CRE-exposed slice and just got hit again on BofA's flat-trading warning. XLF keeps the sector's momentum through insurers, exchanges and diversified banks that benefit from a steeper front end and 5% yields on their float. Sized at 7% because the group was -1.1% this week; 12% stop.

New long: communication services is the only sector positive on the week (+2.95%) and on the month (+2.15%), and it jumped 2.2% on 09-14 to $115.07 as money rotated out of chips into ad-driven platforms and software. It is the group whose one-month momentum is improving while everything else deteriorates, which is exactly what a cross-sectional re-rank should buy. 7% with a 12% stop given its 3M number is still slightly negative.

Cut from 12 to 6, not dropped. Biotech still carries one of the strongest six-month runs in the market (~26% over the past quarter into early September) and remains a top-five non-AI momentum group, but it is long-duration equity facing a 5% ten-year and a hiking Fed, has pulled back ~4% since 09-08 (closing $157.60 on 09-14), and several names drew downgrades this week. Half size respects the rank while limiting rate-shock damage; stop widened to 15% for the group's volatility, take-profit 25%.

Flipped from a 9% long to an 8% short. Industrials are -7.8% on a month and -10.2% on three, the second-worst sector in the tape, with XLI gapping down through $172 and approaching correction territory ($169.93 close on 09-14); transports confirmed a bearish head-and-shoulders and the data-center power/construction complex inside the sector (Eaton -7%, Quanta -4%, GEV -8.6% on 09-14) just lost its AI narrative. Largest short because it is the cleanest broken uptrend. Tight 10% stop because I am entering after a sharp move.

New short: utilities are -6.3% on a month, -7.8% on three and -11.9% on six, the worst six-month sector, and XLU has fallen six sessions straight to $41.78. A 5% ten-year and ~56bp of further hikes priced is the worst possible regime for a bond proxy, and the AI-power-demand story that had been propping the group up cracked on 09-14. 7% with a 10% stop because a dovish Fed surprise would squeeze it hardest, and a 20% take-profit.

Kept, trimmed from 6 to 5, currently +2.85% on the leg. Homebuilders are a named lagging bellwether, XHB is $98.27 from $103.25 a week earlier, and mortgage rates key off a ten-year that just printed its highest level since 2007 while the Fed hikes into it. Trimmed only because the rate-sensitive short cluster (XHB/XLU/XLI) is now 20% of the book and I want the correlation budget spread. 12% stop, 20% take-profit.

Kept, trimmed from 7 to 5, +1.75% on the leg. Consumer cyclical is -4.9% on a month and -7% YTD, retail XRT just had its worst two-day settle in three months, and $105 oil plus a rate hike is a direct squeeze on the discretionary consumer. Smaller because XLY's mega-cap weights (Amazon, Tesla) can rally on tech rebounds independent of the consumer, which is why I pair it with XHB rather than doubling up. 12% stop, 20% take-profit.

Fable Unconstrained.strategy: Defensive risk-premia harvest: long contrarian value/mean-reversion (gold pullback, Brazil carry, UNH, Berkshire, a smaller staples sleeve) plus a small volatility-risk-premium sleeve via SVXY, with 46% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Anchor value leg, unchanged at 16%. $508 vs 52-week range $464-538, $1.09T market cap, Abel has redeployed $39.4B into equities in six months and the float-funded, cash-rich structure is the closest thing to a positive-carry equity when short rates may go up rather than down. Leg +0.4%. No stop: this is the position I want to add to on a drawdown, not be shaken out of.

Contrarian recovery leg, unchanged at 12%. $397-401, 23 buys / 0 sells, Bernstein initiated Buy on Sept 1, Morningstar-style fair values moved to ~$529 on Medicare margin recovery; $2.32 dividend with Sept 14 record date lands inside this leg. Healthcare was the only sector besides energy with positive 1m and 6m momentum, so the value thesis now has a tape behind it. Wide 30% stop is deliberate: the thesis is multi-quarter and the stock gaps on regulatory headlines.

Pullback-buy leg, unchanged at 10%. Gold ~$4,500-4,520, GLD 6m -14% and 20% below its $509 high but 1m +4.4% and back above the 20-day after two up sessions; Waller said he would hold if Sept 11 CPI cools, which took hike odds from 63% to ~50% before the jobs print sent them back up. A confirmed hike is the risk; the Iran escalation and $95 Brent are the offset. Leg -0.4%, nothing to do. No stop: I want to hold this through a hike-driven flush, not sell into it.

Brazil carry leg, trimmed 10% -> 7% and given a +10% take-profit. Up 5.1% on the leg and 6.5% on the week to RSI 69 because polls (PoderData 45-44 Flavio, Datafolha 46-44 Lula) put a market-friendly outcome roughly at coin-flip odds for the Oct 4 first round. That is no longer a contrarian entry; it is a position the market agrees with, so I harvest a third of it and let the rest ride the carry with a mechanical exit if the poll rally overshoots. USD/BRL 5.10 and a weaker DXY (98.97) support the remainder.

Staples defensive sleeve, cut 8% -> 5%. 6m -1.4%, 1m -0.6%, below its 20- and 50-day, RSI 45, and Lululemon's -17% guide cut on Friday is a reminder that the consumer is soft. With the 10-year at 4.76-4.81% a bond-proxy sector has an active headwind, so it keeps only a token weight for its low beta; cash at 4% is the better defensive asset this month.

Volatility-risk-premium sleeve, new at 4%. Spot VIX 14.5 vs Sep future ~16.6, Oct ~18.4, Nov ~19.1: steep contango, so the -0.5x product earns roll as the front future decays toward spot if Sept 11 CPI and the Sept 16 FOMC pass without a shock. The 63%-priced hike is largely in the front future already; the real tail is an Iran/oil escalation, which is why the size is 4% and the stop is 20%, capping a mid-20s VIX spike at about 1% of NAV. This is the one sleeve the strategy of record has named all along and not carried.

Opus-fleet deep value.strategy: Concentrated long in sub-market-multiple, FCF-rich dividend payers barbelled between hard-asset energy (repricing to $103 WTI on stale sell-side estimates) and the cheapest defensives in the market (pharma/managed care at 9-11x) plus a 1.2x-book bank, funded by an enlarged short in 25x consumer-staples bond proxies, with net exposure held flat into the FOMC hike.

positions.thesis: Largest single weight and the book's core hard-asset holding. At $215 it is +45% YTD and +1.9% on my current leg, and the 15.8x forward multiple overstates the price because consensus EPS is anchored to $70-80 oil against a $103.55 print. 3.36% dividend yield backed by genuine free cash flow, not leverage, and the 20 Mtpa LNG buildout across Argentina, the Mediterranean and Australia gives a gas-linked earnings stream that is structurally short of supply in exactly the inflation regime the Fed is now hiking into. Held flat at 15% rather than increased: I want the exposure, but I will not upsize an integrated major into a supply-attack spike after a 45% run.

The deepest value in the book and the purest expression of the mandate: 9.5x forward earnings, a 10.5% earnings yield, and a 6.2% dividend yield. It is DOWN 1.4% today while energy rallies, which is precisely why I am keeping it at full size rather than rotating into what worked this morning -- I am a value manager, not a momentum manager, and selling the 9.5x asset to buy the 15.8x asset on one day's tape would invert my own process. The COVID-revenue cliff and patent expiries are the reason it is cheap and are already in the multiple; oncology and obesity launches are unpriced optionality. Risk I accept: a 6.2% yield is only ~120bp of spread over a 5.01% 10-year, thinner than when I sized this, hence the wide 18% stop to survive rate-driven noise without being shaken out of the cheapest large-cap in the market.

Raised from 10% to 13% and now my preferred energy expression over XOM. As the largest independent E&P it is the highest-torque liquid in the book to the oil price itself, with no refining or chemicals to dilute the upstream beta, and at 13.59x forward it is the only one of my three energy names still inside the 10-13x mandate band. +51.6% YTD and +2.5% on this leg, with UBS at a $169 target versus $138.86 spot. The add is funded by the VZ cut and is deliberately concentrated here rather than spread across the majors, because if the SPR-at-1982-lows supply story is real, the pure E&P captures the most of it. Stop tightened from 20% to 18% to respect that I am adding after a large run.

Held flat at 11%. Still the cheapest way in the book to own a systemically important balance sheet: 10.48x forward and 1.19x book against an average analyst target of $155 versus $138.70 spot, +1.8% today and +1.6% on this leg. A hiking Fed is genuinely good for net interest income on a $6 trillion daily payments franchise. I am deliberately NOT upsizing despite the cheapness, because the same 5% 10-year that fattens NII also marks down the securities portfolio and raises credit-loss risk, and the mounting-federal-debt narrative that drove yields to 2007 highs is not a benign backdrop for a global bank. Cheap enough to own, ambiguous enough not to press.

Raised from 8% to 10%. At 11.3x forward with a 2.78% yield and an average target of $116 against $94.19 spot, this is cheap defensive cash flow rather than expensive defensive cash flow -- the long leg of the value spread whose short leg is XLP. Down 1.4% today alongside the rest of healthcare and -1.4% on my leg, which is the add opportunity: the Health Services margin pressure and PBM regulatory overhang are well known and discounted, while the integrated pharmacy/insurance/primary-care franchise generates real FCF that does not depend on the rate cycle. Sized below PFE because the regulatory tail is genuinely fatter.

Doubled from 4% to 8% and the highest-conviction change in this book. At 24.75x trailing earnings with a 2.59% dividend yield, consumer staples are being asked to compete with a 5.01% risk-free rate while a Fed under Warsh hikes into persistent inflation -- an investor is paid half the Treasury yield to own no-growth equity risk at a market-premium multiple. It is already down 0.96% today and +0.45% for me on this leg. At 4% the hedge was too small to change the book's outcome; at 8% it actually offsets. This is also the short leg of a clean, largely rate-neutral value spread against my 9-11x pharma longs: long cheap defensives, short expensive defensives. The 10% stop is deliberately tight because staples outperform in an equity drawdown and I do not want this hedge to become the loss.

Raised from 7% to 8%. 9.81x forward with a 3.93% yield puts it alongside PFE as the cheapest large-cap pharma available, and positive Phase 2 CAR-T data is a real pipeline catalyst that the multiple gives no credit for. Down 1.2% today with the healthcare complex and -1.9% on my leg, so the modest add is buying weakness in an asset whose valuation floor is set by cash flow rather than sentiment. Kept smaller than PFE and CVS because the Eliquis patent cliff is the nearest-dated and most quantifiable revenue hole in the book; the 16% stop is the tightest of my pharma legs for that reason.

Raised from 5% to 7% on one specific, non-oil-price catalyst: record refining margins driven by global fuel shortages, which is a downstream earnings stream that does NOT reverse if the Saudi supply disruption is repaired and crude backs off. That makes XOM the diversifying energy holding rather than a duplicate of COP's pure upstream beta. +41.7% YTD and my best leg at +3.1%. Kept the smallest of the three energy names because 15.13x forward is the furthest above my 10-13x mandate band and a $167.20 price sits essentially on the $170.91 average target, leaving little analyst-anchored room. Stop held at 15%.

Opus-fleet dividend growth.strategy: Long-only dividend-growth book anchored by a 34% SCHD core and deliberately tilted into hard-asset dividend aristocrats - integrated oil majors and midstream - funded by exiting the most expensive bond-proxy staple and a pharma leg with a sector overhang, because a 5% 10-year Treasury has repriced every low-yield defensive while a $103 oil shock pays the energy dividend growers directly.

positions.thesis: The chassis of the mandate and still the highest-conviction single line: a 0.06% ER screen for 10-year dividend consistency plus quality (ROE, cash-flow-to-debt) that is up ~26% YTD against SPY's ~11%, i.e. the dividend/value factor is winning this year by roughly 16 points and I want to keep owning that beta rather than hand-pick around it. Its 0.56 five-year beta and sector mix - energy, staples, health care, financials - is the same regime bet I am making with the single names, so the core and the satellites compound rather than fight. Trimmed 36 to 34 only to fund the energy add; no take-profit because a core holding should not be stopped out of a working factor by a number I picked in advance. 12% stop is a regime-break stop, not a noise stop.

The purest expression of the mandate in this macro: a 38-year dividend grower paying 3.36% - above the 10-year's 5% on an after-growth basis and rising - at 15.8x forward earnings while WTI sits at $103. Raised 12 to 15 because the oil move is supply-driven (Saudi pipeline outage, SPR at 1982 lows), which flows to the integrated model's upstream margin without the demand destruction that usually caps an oil rally, and because management is explicitly building for it: 20 Mtpa of LNG capacity targeted across Argentina, the Mediterranean and Australia, into a world short of fuel. BMO raised its target to $235 on 2026-09-03. Sized at 15 rather than larger because $215 is already ~45% YTD and near the $221 consensus average, so I am paying up for a regime, not a discount. 12% stop is deliberately wide - this is a headline-driven commodity name and a Middle East de-escalation is the live risk - and the 20% take-profit harvests the melt-up rather than the peak.

New leg, added specifically so the 28% energy tilt is not a single-balance-sheet bet. A 43-year consecutive dividend raiser at 15.1x forward with a 2.5% yield, and up 41.7% YTD on a different driver than CVX: refining and product margins are being held up by global fuel shortages, which is the downstream side of the same shock that lifts CVX's upstream. That decorrelation within energy is the entire reason for holding both - if crude mean-reverts but product cracks stay tight, XOM carries the sleeve, and the reverse holds for CVX. Piper Sandler just took its target from $158 to $185 against a $167 price. Sized at 8, half of CVX, because CVX is the higher-yielding and longer-tenured dividend grower and remains the sleeve's anchor; XOM is the diversifier, not the co-lead. Same 12/20 stop/target frame as CVX since it is the same underlying risk factor.

Held at 8 and now the largest health-care leg after AMGN exits. It is the winner of the current leg at +4.19% and it carries the Abbott dividend heritage - 53 consecutive years of increases across the spin - which is exactly the 25-year-plus pedigree the mandate is built on. Pharma is the one defensive I am keeping weight in through a 5% 10-year, because unlike a staple its pricing is contractual and patent-protected rather than a function of consumer elasticity, so it does not get squeezed from both ends by the oil shock the way KO does. Immunology has cleared the Humira cliff and the Skyrizi/Rinvoq ramp is the growth that funds continued raises. Stop at 10% and target 18% - a clinical or policy shock in pharma is a fast, discrete repricing, so a tighter stop than the energy legs is appropriate.

A 48-year dividend grower and the book's medtech exposure, trimmed 8 to 7 as partial funding for the energy add. Kept because procedure volumes are the least macro-sensitive revenue line I own - hospital capital and elective procedure demand does not care about the 10-year or the oil price - which is genuine diversification against a book that is now 28% levered to crude. It is modestly profitable on the leg at +0.94% and trades at a discount to its medtech peers, so I am not paying a premium for that diversification. Trimmed rather than exited because the diversification is the point; 15% take-profit is lower than the energy legs because the realistic bull case here is multiple normalization, not a commodity move.

The 63-year dividend king and one of two remaining AAA-rated corporate balance sheets in the United States. Held at 6 through a -2.03% leg because this is the position whose job is to still be there and still be raising if the FOMC turns genuinely hawkish tomorrow and the market repricing is disorderly - a AAA credit is the one equity that does not need the funding markets to stay open. It is the cheapest form of ballast I can own inside a long-only dividend mandate, strictly better than adding to the 4% cash line for that purpose because it still compounds a growing dividend. No take-profit, because a ballast leg should never be sold into strength; a 10% stop is there only for a company-specific event such as an adverse talc or Stelara-erosion development.

Held flat at 5 - not raised - as the book's deliberate rate-beneficiary. At 11.0x forward and a 3.45% yield just increased 3.8%, it is the cheapest thing I own, and a higher-for-longer or hiking Fed widens net interest margin on the asset side. I am explicitly NOT sizing it up despite that, because USB is the same bank whose securities book blew a hole in tangible capital via AOCI the last time the long end moved this fast, and a 10-year that has gone from 4.3% to 5.01% reopens exactly that mark-to-market wound. Holding 5% keeps the rate-hedge leg in the book while acknowledging the position is long NIM and short duration at the same time. 12% stop reflects that two-sided risk; the 20% target reflects the 12% discount to the $70 consensus average.

Raised 3 to 5. The one leg in the book that competes with a 5% Treasury on the Treasury's own terms - a 5.70% distribution yield, backed by 27 consecutive years of distribution growth, at 12.2x forward with adjusted EBITDA up 17% year on year. Midstream is the right way to add energy beta on top of CVX and XOM rather than a third producer, because EPD's 50,000 miles of pipe earns fee-based, largely volume- and often inflation-escalated revenue: it gets paid for throughput whether crude is $103 or $80, so it holds up in precisely the de-escalation scenario that would hurt the two majors. That is why it earns a raise even though Morgan Stanley is Underweight it. Kept at 5 rather than larger because K-1 midstream is structurally less liquid and because 28% total energy is already the ceiling I am willing to run.

Opus-fleet price momentum.strategy: Concentrated long-only US price momentum rotated out of the broken memory/AI-hardware and rate-sensitive biotech themes and into the only complex actually printing new 52-week highs into 2026-09-15 - refining and the crude/product squeeze - with a secondary sleeve in the hardware-to-software rotation leaders, trend-break stops on every leg.

positions.thesis: Closed at a 52-week high today (+2.0%), +14.3% over 1m, +58.0% over 3m, +140% over 12m - its best run since 1982 - and sits 18.5% above its 50dma with the trend still accelerating rather than rolling. Valero is the purest listed expression of the tight global refined-product market driving this move: Gulf Coast complexity means it captures the distillate crack that is up 53% over 3m. Largest single leg because it is the highest-conviction new-high name in the entire screen, and it is already in the book so I pay no round-trip to keep it.

Strongest 3-month refining momentum of the majors at +60.8% and +76.2% over 6m, closing at a 52-week high today, 19.3% above its 50dma. Marathon has the largest US refining system by throughput, so it carries the most absolute leverage to the crack widening, and its MPLX stake gives a midstream cash-flow floor if crude backs off. Held at near-max refining weight as the second core leg of the theme.

At a 52-week high, +12.2% 1m and +51.3% 3m, 16.7% above its 50dma - the least-extended of the three integrated refiners I hold, which is why it takes the smaller of the three core weights. Its midstream and chemicals segments dilute pure crack leverage slightly, so it functions as the lower-beta member of the refining sleeve while still participating in the trend.

New addition. At a 52-week high with +17.2% over 1m - faster than any of VLO/MPC/PSX - and +63.3% 3m, +94.0% 6m. HF Sinclair is a mid-continent refiner whose inland crude sourcing gives it a wider realized margin than coastal peers when WTI-linked feedstock lags the product move, so it is the highest-torque way to add refining exposure without doubling down on a name I already own. Slightly wider stop than the majors to respect the higher single-name volatility.

New addition as deliberate ballast inside the energy theme. XLE closed at a 52-week high but is only 7.9% above its 50dma versus 17-19% for my refining legs, so it carries the same directional trend at roughly half the extension. It also shifts part of my energy weight from crack-spread dependence to producers (XOM, CVX both at or near highs), which is the exposure that survives if product margins mean-revert while crude stays bid. Tight 10% stop because a diversified ETF that breaks 10% has broken the theme.

New addition. Product tanker rates are the physical confirmation of the refined-product dislocation: STNG closed at a 52-week high, +9.2% 1m, and sits only 10.2% above its 50dma - the cleanest, least-parabolic entry in the tanker group. Owning the shipping leg means I profit from the product imbalance itself rather than from any one refiner's margin capture. Small weight and a wide 18% stop because tanker equities routinely draw down 15% inside an intact uptrend.

New addition, smallest energy leg. Frontline is the fastest-moving name on the entire board at +12.7% on the week and +27.5% on the month, at a 52-week high, and VLCC rates are the highest-beta claim on crude being physically moved. It is 26.8% above its 50dma, which is parabolic, so it gets a 3% weight and a 20% stop - I want the convexity if the squeeze extends and a capped loss if it snaps.

New addition and the largest non-energy leg. +25.5% over 3m and +9.5% above its 50dma while QQQ is -4.7% over 3m and SMH is -15.4% - that is textbook relative-strength leadership, not beta. The specific driver is the rotation the tape is running right now: as AI-pacing concerns hammer chips, capital is moving into the software and cloud layer that monetizes AI without owning the capex cycle. Sized at 10% as the cleanest way to stay long the AI complex from the side that is still making progress.

The one AI-hardware position I keep, and the reason is purely price: it closed 0.65% off its 52-week high, +5.5% today, +14.8% 1m and +260% 6m, while every memory and networking peer I screened is 24-49% off its high. Post-earnings breakouts that hold while the whole peer group breaks are the strongest momentum signal available. Trimmed from 8% to 7% because theme-level guilt by association is a real risk, and the 18% stop reflects its realized volatility.

New addition on a fresh momentum inflection: +9.2% on the week and +13.6% on the month, the best 1-month print in mega-cap tech, turning up out of a base after a weak 12 months. It is still 14.1% below its 52-week high, so this is early-stage trend rather than a chase, and it is 10.9% above its 50dma confirming the turn is real. Sized at 6% precisely because the base is unproven relative to my energy legs.

New addition. +8.1% 1m, +11.6% 3m, and only 2.76% off its 52-week high - a steady, low-drawdown uptrend at a moment when the rest of large-cap tech is choppy. Apple has minimal AI-capex exposure, so it does not share the chip complex's downside, and its cash generation makes it relatively indifferent to a hawkish Fed. It is the lowest-volatility momentum leg available, hence the tight 10% stop.

New addition and the direct replacement for the XBI/AMGN biotech sleeve I am cutting. ABBV is +16.7% over 3m and only 2.75% off its 52-week high, versus XBI 9.1% off its high and below its 50dma and AMGN 15.2% off its high. Large-cap pharma with near-term cash flows is far less duration-sensitive than unprofitable small-cap biotech, which matters specifically because the 2026-09-16 FOMC is being priced for a hike with the 10-year at 5.00%. Keeps the healthcare exposure that is working and drops the part that is not.

Opus-fleet quality compounders.strategy: Concentrated long book of five wide-moat, high-ROIC, net-cash compounders - GOOGL, V, NVDA, TSM, META - rebalanced away from second-derivative AI-capex exposure toward cash-generative and nominal-spend-linked franchises, with a 16% cash buffer earning 4% against a Fed that is hiking into a 5% ten-year.

positions.thesis: Largest position and the best regime fit in the book. Alphabet is an AI USER, not an AI-capex supplier, so the pacing call that just repriced the semis complex is neutral-to-positive for it: if hyperscaler buildout paces, Google's depreciation burden eases and free cash flow improves, while Search keeps earning enormous cash TODAY rather than in a terminal year that a 5% discount rate punishes. It is the only leg of the outgoing book in the green (+2.13%), it is still 15% below its 52-week high, and it carries roughly $95bn of net cash so a hiking Fed costs it nothing on the liability side. Cloud is compounding on real enterprise wins (Salesforce partnership expansion, new Singapore engineering centre this week). Trimmed two points only to fund the new legs, not on any change of view. The 18% stop is wider than the name's realised volatility because I want it to survive a macro drawdown, not a macro wobble.

positions.thesis: This is the single best expression of the house view and I am sizing it accordingly, up from 34%. JAAA holds 90%+ AAA CLO tranches at roughly a 5.0-5.6% yield with near-zero duration, so its coupon mechanically resets higher off term SOFR when the Fed takes the funds rate to 3.75-4.00% tomorrow - it is one of the few carry assets that gets paid MORE by the event that is 85-90% priced, and it takes essentially no mark-to-market hit if the dots come out more hawkish still. Critically, it is the opposite side of the trade I am exiting in CLOZ: AAA sits at the very top of the CLO waterfall with the entire mezzanine and equity stack subordinated beneath it, so the CCC/single-B dispersion and private-credit gating that is chewing through junior tranches has to destroy an implausible amount of collateral before it reaches this paper. Street base case has Tier 1 AAA new issue around S+125, in line with current levels, so I am not paying up for the spread either. A $27bn fund gives me the liquidity to hold a 46% weight without it being a position I cannot exit. Stop at 5% is a true circuit breaker, not a trading stop - JAAA's worst historical drawdown is in the 2-3% area, so a 5% break would mean a systemic liquidity dislocation in structured credit and I want to be out mechanically if that happens rather than arguing with it.

Held and nudged up a point, because this leg is doing a job no other position in the book can do. At a 7.3% trailing distribution yield it is the highest-carry asset I own, and the source of that carry is fee-based US midstream cash flow tied to volumes, storage and long-term contracts rather than to the spot crude print - which matters right now, with WTI having slipped under $70 on soft demand even while the Iran conflict keeps a geopolitical risk premium in the curve. More importantly it is the natural hedge to the very thing forcing the Fed's hand: the August CPI beat was driven by energy, gasoline up 3.9% and the energy index up 2.1%, accounting for over a third of the headline gain. If that energy shock persists or worsens, the Fed hikes further and every other leg in this book just earns a higher reset coupon while AMLP also appreciates. If the shock fades, the Fed backs off and I keep collecting 7.3%. That two-sided payoff is why it stays at a fifth of the book. This is now my only real equity-beta leg, so I have tightened the stop from 18% to 15% - a 15% drawdown would mean the fee-based thesis itself has broken rather than just oil being noisy - and kept the 25% take-profit, which is roughly where a geopolitical supply spike would take midstream before I would rather bank it than press it.

Kept and sized up one point, as the investment-grade half of the floating-rate core. FLOT yields roughly 4.6% on floating-rate IG corporate paper with near-zero duration, so like JAAA it gets a coupon uplift from tomorrow's hike rather than a price hit, and it diversifies the book's credit exposure away from being purely structured: JAAA's risk is the broadly syndicated loan collateral pool, FLOT's is investment-grade corporate balance sheets, and those two do not fail together in any scenario short of a genuine recession. It is also the deliberate quality substitute for the CLOZ weight I am retiring - I want to keep the book's spread income, I just want to earn it from IG issuers rather than from the levered loan tail where the CCC/single-B differential has already gapped 200bp wider this year. 12% is a supporting weight, not a bet; the 5% stop matches the JAAA logic, since IG floaters only move that far in a real credit event.

SPYI writes S&P index calls to convert implied volatility into a high monthly distribution, and the variance premium is structurally richest into a scheduled macro event, which is exactly what a 2pm FOMC decision plus a Warsh press conference is. The payoff shape also happens to fit the house view: with a hike 85-90% priced, the upside scenario for equities is a modest relief rally rather than a melt-up, and giving away the tail above the strike costs me little while the premium collected is real. I am keeping it deliberately small because it is the one leg in the book that carries genuine equity drawdown risk without a floating coupon underneath it, and at 6% a bad quarter here cannot meaningfully damage NAV. The 12% stop is unchanged and sits below any normal index correction, so it only triggers on a proper risk-off break where I would want the cash back anyway.
