The reason for the size cut is honest: 2026 is a guided trough production year at about 5.26Moz on mine sequencing, and the same oil surge that helps SLB pushes Newmont's AISC above roughly $1,700/oz through diesel, so this leg is short the oil factor that SLB is long. That internal offset is a feature - it keeps the pair's shared macro loading near zero - but it caps how much either can carry. 20% stop, 35% take-profit.

Held, cut from 5.0% to 3.7%. The residual is the North American natural gas cost advantage: global nitrogen prices are set by the European gas-based marginal producer, so an energy shock that lifts European gas widens CF's spread even as it compresses competitors'. That makes it a second, structurally different way to be long the energy disruption than SLB - one is activity-driven, the other is cost-curve-driven - which is why they can coexist without breaching the pairwise correlation limit. Trimmed because it shares an agricultural end-market with DE and I do not want two full-weight ag-linked legs. 18% stop.

New, and the most orthogonal residual in the book: the earnings driver is Macau gross gaming revenue and Singapore Marina Bay Sands, which responds to Chinese travel policy and regional visitation, not to the FOMC, the ten-year, or AI capex. The stock is down 34.6% year to date on post-Q2 margin disappointment, yet Sands China's mass GGR grew 8% against a 4% market - the operating share gain is intact while the multiple is not. Management is voting with capital: $787m repurchased in Q2, the authorization raised to $6.0bn, and the Sands China stake lifted above 75.1% on 2026-09-01. Sized at 3.7%, not full weight, because a 34.6% drawdown name has high residual volatility and the vol-tempering rule caps it; 20% stop and 35% take-profit to bound a leg whose repricing is discontinuous.

Held but cut from 4.5% to 3.2% - the smallest surviving equity weight, and the cut is the thesis. The broadband subscriber and convergence argument is still genuinely idiosyncratic, which is why it stays as the communication-services sleeve. But Charter runs high leverage, and at a 5% ten-year with a hawkish chair the refinancing arithmetic is a real headwind that a SPY short does not hedge. I am unwilling to carry full size in a levered balance sheet into a hiking decision, so I keep a reduced stake for sector coverage and residual diversification rather than exit a thesis that has not actually been falsified. 20% stop.

Held at the smallest weight in the book (+2.17% on the prior leg). Clinical-stage biotech is the purest residual available - outcomes are decided by trial readouts and regulatory decisions that are uncorrelated with the funds rate, the index and every other leg here, which is exactly what drives the basket's average pairwise correlation down. It is also the highest-volatility name I own, so volatility-tempering forces it to 2.8% even though its diversification value is the highest per dollar. Wide 25% stop and 45% take-profit because binary readouts move this stock in gaps that a normal stop would simply convert into a realized loss at the worst price.

The hedge, sized mechanically rather than directionally. The rescreened basket carries an estimated beta contribution of about 0.75 (up from 0.66 on the prior basket, because SLB, LVS, CF and GPN add beta faster than CME, MCK and DG remove it), so 0.75 x 54.7% of long gross calls for roughly 41% of NAV short and I set 40.3%, leaving net index beta of about +1% of NAV - close enough to zero that index direction should not decide this book's return. Raising the short from 38% is not a bearish call on the FOMC: if I wanted that view I would take it in the net, and I do not, because my mandate is to earn the cross-sectional residual and let the index wash out. I attach no stop-loss to this leg deliberately - a stop on the hedge would fire precisely in a melt-up and leave a 54.7% long basket naked, converting a market-neutral book into a directional one at the worst possible moment. Short borrow at 3% APR on 40.3% of NAV is about 121bp annualized, roughly a third of which is recovered by 4% APY on the 5% cash, and it is the correct price for owning dispersion rather than direction in a week when the S&P moved 0.48% while semis moved 5.9%.

Opus 5 event driven.strategy: A concentrated event book rebuilt around the one hard-dated, beta-immune catalyst that still pays — the post-vote ACA/CRH cash merger — plus a live physical-supply event in energy, two post-earnings-drift legs whose estimate revisions still point the right way, and a reduced index short now that the September hike is fully priced.

positions.thesis: The best risk-adjusted asset I can own in this tape and the reason to enlarge it from 18% to 33%. CRH is acquiring Arcosa for $150.00 per share in all cash; stockholders approved on 2026-09-04 by 39,595,867 to 66,113 — a 99.8% margin — so the vote condition is gone and only customary regulatory clearance remains, with close guided to Q1 2027. At the $145.10 mark that is a 3.38% gross spread over roughly four and a half months, about 9% annualized, against a cash consideration that does not care about the 10Y at 5.02%, Brent at $108, or what Powell says at 2:30pm on Wednesday. That last point is the whole argument for the size: every other risk in this book is macro-correlated and this leg has a beta of approximately zero to all of it. Aggregates M&A carries limited overlap risk and the 2026 backdrop has been unusually permissive, with the HFRI merger arb index +8.2% on faster completions and fewer breaks. Sized at 33% rather than higher because a break is the single point of failure: the unaffected price implies roughly -22% on a bust, and the 8% stop caps that at about -2.6% of NAV. Take-profit at 3.5% above my 2026-09-16 fill sits essentially at the $150 deal price, so the leg retires itself on convergence instead of sitting in dead money into 2027.

The most tape-datable live event on the board, and the only long I can own that is helped rather than hurt by the two forces wrecking the rest of the market. This is a physical supply event, not a sentiment one: Hormuz crude flows are below 2mbpd against 8-9mbpd pre-conflict, inventories are drawing, tanker strikes have continued through the El Gaia hit near Hengam Island, and Brent settled near $108 after its strongest weekly rally since 2022. The dated catalyst is the negative one: the Salalah GCC-Iran ministerial on 2026-09-14 was the week's only scheduled event capable of taking risk premium out of the barrel and Oman postponed it with no new date after Saudi Arabia objected to the Iran-Oman corridor amendments and Bahrain declined to attend. The de-escalation path got structurally worse, not better, and crude rose ~2% on the postponement alone. I am buying the equity rather than crude because energy producers have lagged the move in the barrel and because equity does not gap the way the front month does. I hold this at 14% and not larger precisely because the headline risk is two-sided and violent — Brent has printed -10% days on nothing more than Trump delaying strikes — and because it is directionally correlated with, not hedged against, my index short. The 12% stop respects that a genuine ceasefire headline is a gap risk no stop fully protects against, so position size is the real risk control here.

The one post-earnings-drift leg I am keeping at close to full size, because it is the only one where the fundamental support behind the gap is still strengthening rather than decaying. Salesforce beat and raised on its late-August print, the gap has been held rather than given back, the leg is +3.5% for me, and critically the FY2027 consensus has been revised UP by four cents over the past 30 days to $14.16, implying 13.1% year-over-year growth. That upward revision trend is what distinguishes a drift that has further to run from a gap that is simply decaying, and it is the specific evidence I am underwriting. The stock is +42.5% over three months so I am respecting that some of the recent weakness is profit-taking in a rate-driven software selloff rather than anything company-specific. I have trimmed from 12% to 9% rather than holding size because a 5.02% 10Y compresses multiples on every long-duration cash flow regardless of how good the revisions are, and I would rather carry the drift smaller than defend it. Take-profit added at 18% to retire the leg on convergence instead of holding it into the next print.

My best-performing leg at +8.28%, and I am trimming it from 9% to 6% and putting a take-profit on it rather than letting a winner run, because the fundamental case underneath the drift has quietly turned. The Zacks FY2027 consensus for Atlassian has been revised DOWN seven cents in the past seven days to $5.69, implying a 2.7% year-over-year DECLINE in EPS, and the shares are -4.1% over twelve months. A post-earnings drift held on negative revisions into a 5% 10Y and an AI-capex narrative shock is a momentum position wearing a catalyst's clothes. The correct handling is to bank most of what the drift has already paid and leave a small residual with a tightened 10% stop and a take-profit at 9% above my fill, which is within reach of the move already in hand. This leg is now a position I am exiting on a schedule, not one I am adding to.

Re-based and reduced, not removed. The thesis this leg was originally sized for — that a September hike was roughly a coin flip and therefore underpriced — is dead: fed funds futures are ~92% for 25bp, and my fill at the 2026-09-16 close lands after the decision and the presser, so there is no event premium left for me to capture. What survives is a different and still-live argument: the Fed is tightening into a war-driven oil supply shock, the 10Y is at 5.02% and its highest since 2007, Brent is at $108, and the President has publicly threatened to reshape trade policy if the Fed hikes. That is a multiple-compression regime regardless of Wednesday's outcome, and this leg is now sized as a beta hedge against my remaining 29% of long equity exposure in CRM, TEAM and XLE rather than as a directional macro bet. Cut from 9% to 8% and given a 7% stop specifically because the live risk after a fully-priced hike is a sell-the-rumor-buy-the-news relief rally, and I want a mechanical exit if the index tells me this hedge has become the wrong trade.

Opus 5 mean reversion.strategy: Re-ranked the liquid US large-cap universe through the 2026-09-14 close and rebuilt around a single discipline: buy oversold quality whose drawdown cause is ALREADY PRICED into Wednesday's Fed decision (rate-sensitive and beta washouts), refuse oversold names whose drawdown cause is live and unpriced (the 3-day-old AI-pacing shock and the $100 oil/Hormuz shock), keep a small short in the crowded AI-hardware winner, and hold 16% cash at 4% as dry powder across the first Fed hike since 2023.

positions.thesis: Largest leg and the cleanest setup in my universe. Down ~34% over a year and within ~8% of its $366 52-week low, but the bear case that caused the de-rate -- the Design IP segment shrinking all year -- inflected in the Q3 print on 08-26, with Design IP back to ~11% y/y growth at $474mm. That is a multiple de-rate on improving fundamentals, which is precisely the case my mandate says to keep rather than discard. It also has a dated catalyst inside my holding window: the 09-30 Investor Day, where IP royalty and AI-monetisation detail is what 19 of 25 covering analysts rating Buy or better are waiting on. At ~26x NTM versus CDNS at ~40x it is the cheaper half of the EDA pair, so it absorbs the Kimi K3 EDA-disruption narrative and a 5% 10Y with far less multiple to lose. Sized up from 11% on the strength of the catalyst; the wide 18% stop is deliberate because this is a high-beta name I need to hold through a Fed day to reach 09-30.

Trimmed from 15% because it has already done part of its work (+0.57% on the old leg) and so is a less coy reversion candidate than it was, but kept as the book's largest defensive anchor. Medtech procedure volumes are the one demand stream in my book that is indifferent to both live macro drivers: hospital capital and elective procedure schedules do not reprice on a 25bp fed funds move and do not carry a fuel bill. In a book whose other longs all have some rate or geopolitical beta, I want a genuinely uncorrelated 12% rather than more cash.

I am being honest that this leg has changed character: I bought it on 09-08 as a bottom-decile loser, and it has since converted into a momentum position with a live catalyst -- the US-Iran conflict running since February, strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure, fresh sell-side upgrades on LMT specifically, and institutional flow into defense ETFs. A purist would exit a thesis that converted. I size it up instead, because it is the only long in the book that is positively exposed to the oil-and-geopolitics factor that is the direct cause of the drawdowns in everything else I own. It is a deliberate internal hedge: if Hormuz worsens, HD and GS and SNPS all get worse and this gets better. Only +1% of size, because paying up for a crowded safety trade is how mean-reversion books get hurt.

Held flat at 9% -- the only leg I neither trimmed nor added to, because the original thesis is simply unfinished. It is -3.41% since the 09-08 entry, so the reversion has not been paid out, and nothing in either regime break invalidates the cause: the drawdown was newsless multiple compression in a diversified industrial, not a demand break. Its aerospace and defense segment gives it the same geopolitical offset as LMT and GD without the crowding, and its short-cycle automation revenue is not a long-duration cash-flow stream that a 5% discount rate mechanically destroys.

Same defense-cycle logic as LMT and up 1% for the same reason, but held as a separate leg rather than folded into LMT because its mix is materially different: Gulfstream business jets and Marine Systems submarine work are long-dated program revenue that is insulated from the Middle East headline cycle, so it gives me defense-budget exposure with less of LMT's day-to-day geopolitical beta. Essentially flat since entry (-0.25%), so unlike LMT I am not paying up for a move that already happened.

Held flat at 8% as low-duration ballast. It is working (+1.76%) and it is the one technology holding whose cash flows are mostly near-term maintenance and subscription renewals rather than terminal-value optionality, so a 5% 10Y does far less damage to its multiple than to any AI-narrative name. Its networking and security demand also does not depend on frontier-model capability improving -- an industry that voluntarily paces capability development still runs and defends the same enterprise networks. The tight 11/14 stop-and-target pair reflects that this is a low-volatility carry leg, not a deep-value swing.

New leg and the purest expression of my priced-versus-unpriced rule. HD sold off with the rest of the housing complex on 09-14 (down more than 1.5% alongside LOW, with LGI -2.5% and TREX -3%) for one identifiable reason: mortgage rates at ~6.76% and the 10Y touching 5%. That is a discount-rate de-rate on an unchanged business -- newsless de-risking, which my mandate keeps -- and crucially the cause gets fully repriced at 2pm on my entry date. A 25bp hike delivered as the ~92% consensus already expects, especially if the statement frames it as the end of the adjustment, removes the overhang that created the drawdown. Large-cap, deeply liquid, dividend-paying, and oil-neutral, so it carries none of the fuel-cost exposure that made me cut RCL. The 13% stop bounds the hawkish-dot-plot scenario at roughly 1% of NAV.

New leg, and the most newsless drawdown on the tape: GS was the second-worst Dow performer on 09-14 at -3.99% with no company-specific item, purely macro beta from the yield and oil moves. That is textbook bottom-decile-for-no-reason. What makes it better than a generic beta bounce is that the macro driver punishing it is arguably a revenue tailwind for it: a first hike in three years, a 5% 10Y and this much rate and commodity volatility is exactly the environment in which the FICC trading franchise earns, and higher rates lift net interest income. So I own a name whose price fell on an input that improves its earnings -- a genuine dislocation rather than a hopeful one. The wider 14% stop respects that financials gap hard if the dot plot implies a hiking cycle rather than a single move.

The mandated short in the crowded top-decile AI-hardware winner, carried and sized up modestly from 6%. It is now the coherent way for this book to express the 09-12 AI-pacing shock: I refuse to buy the semiconductor dip because that shock is three days old and unexhausted, and the consistent other side of that view is to be short the crowded AI-hardware beneficiary rather than long it. DELL is the right vehicle because its AI-server backlog is the most narrative-dependent, lowest-margin part of the AI trade -- a deliberate slowdown in frontier training compresses the order book that justifies its re-rating, while the commodity PC business underneath carries no premium. Kept small at 7% and with an 18% stop because the leg is currently against me (-2.46%), DELL has not yet broken with the group, and a 3% borrow cost is cheap enough to be patient but not free.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Two measured relative-value pairs (XLI/VTV, STLD/NUE) run at 60% gross with 40% cash at 4% - the only legs of the prior five-pair screen whose dislocation still survives the mandate's own fresh-fundamental-catalyst filter now that the Fed has pivoted from cutting to hiking, with the three pairs that were unintentionally a single long-cyclical/small/momentum versus short-defensive-value factor bet removed rather than averaged into.

positions.thesis: Sized UP from 9.8 because this is the one broad pair the catalyst filter does not disqualify, and its spread got better, not worse. Since the 9/8 fill XLI is -2.63% against VTV -0.89%, so the log spread widened another ~1.75% on top of a 2.2-3.4 sigma entry, with only 6 of a measured 10-26 day half-life elapsed - closing that now would be selling at the widest point, the classic pairs error. Critically, the reason I keep this one and drop ITA and MTUM is dilution of catalyst risk: XLI spreads the AI-capex/power shock across ~70 industrials, whereas GE alone is 22% of ITA and semis dominate MTUM's current book, so no single holding's news can drive this spread. The measured daily-return correlation with VTV is the highest-quality relationship in the original screen (two broad US equity baskets, ~70 versus ~330 names), which is what makes the residual genuinely mean-reverting rather than a factor tilt in disguise.

Hedge leg, sized at a 1.286 short/long ratio to XLI - inside the 1.35 cap, so the position still tracks the measured 1:1 log spread while cancelling XLI's higher beta. I am fading VTV's 0.89% outperformance because I can attribute it to two specific and stretched things rather than to an earnings change: VTV's energy weight is being marked up by WTI at $101.39 on a Saudi pipeline supply disruption, which is the most mean-reverting kind of oil move, and its healthcare/staples weight caught the 9/14 defensive bid (XLV, XLP and XLC were the only green sectors) into an FOMC that is already ~90% priced for a hike. A fully-priced hawkish event is exactly the setup where the defensive leg gives back on resolution. No stop: a 12% adverse move in a 330-name value ETF is a market event, and that is when I most need this hedge against XLI still on.

Sized UP from 6.8 to the largest long in the book because this is the only pair in the original five that is genuinely factor-matched, and the tape proved it: while the other four pairs lost 0.10-0.15% of NAV each this week, STLD/NUE lost 0.099% and NUE moved -0.04%, i.e. it behaved as designed while the macro bets did not. Both legs are EAF minimills selling into the same hot-rolled coil curve - HRC fell below $800/short ton in late August and is now rebounding on mill price increases, extended lead times and tariff-reduced imports - so oil at $101, the 10-year at 5% and tomorrow's Fed decision hit both legs almost identically and cancel in the spread. That is precisely the property IJR/IWD and MTUM/XLK lacked. The divergence I am fading is same-industry and idiosyncratic: NUE +49% YTD versus STLD +34% YTD on shared end-market economics, with STLD additionally ramping value-added flat-rolled capacity (two paint, two galvanising lines) at Sinton, TX. No fresh fundamental catalyst on the leg being faded; earnings are 10/19 (NUE 10/26), outside the half-life window. 12% stop because a single-name leg carries real blow-up risk that an ETF leg does not - both names typically guide in the same mid-to-late September window, so that event is largely common-mode and partly cancels in the spread, but the stop is there in case it does not.

Hedge leg at a 1.154 short/long ratio to STLD, well inside the 1.35 cap - tighter than the ETF pair because the two steel names have near-identical betas and near-identical commodity exposure, so less cross-hedge is needed to neutralise. I am short the leg that has run: NUE is +49% YTD at $242.96 on a $54.99bn cap versus STLD +34% at $227.12 on $32.53bn, and the marks show NUE essentially unchanged (+0.04%) while STLD gave back 1.50% since 9/8, which is the spread widening in my favour for re-entry rather than a thesis breaking. Industry-level headwinds - muted demand, sluggish China property, soft residential construction and autos - apply to both legs equally and are not a reason to prefer one. 12% stop for the same single-name blow-up reason as the long leg; no take-profit on either leg, because a take-profit would close one side of the pair and leave me naked in the other, which is the opposite of what this book is for.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: Calendar-driven book running the statistically worst four weeks of the year (Sep 8 to the midterm-year autumn low in early October) at deliberately low gross: keep only legs where the seasonal statistic and the 2026-09-16 rate-hike/energy-shock catalyst point the same way (short intermediate Treasuries, short the utilities bond proxy, long financials and energy, small gold hedge), and carry 46% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 rotation into the midterm-year Q4 rally.

positions.thesis: Highest-conviction leg and the only one where both filters agree with no caveat, so it gets the largest weight (up from 14%). September is historically the worst month of the year for Treasuries, and the 2026 catalyst points the same way: ~90% odds of a 25bp hike on 2026-09-16, August CPI accelerating, WTI near $105, and a WTI/10y correlation of ~0.96 that turns every oil headline into a yield headline. The 10y is already at its highest since 2007 and the marginal risk from Wednesday is the dot plot, which skews hawkish with headline inflation reaccelerating. IEF carries roughly 7 years of duration, so the 6% stop only trips on a ~85bp yield collapse, which realistically requires an Iran ceasefire; that is the acknowledged kill-risk on this leg and 18% at -6% costs about 1.1% of NAV. Short borrow is 3% APR, cheap against the carry of being short a falling bond.

Direct inversion of last week's long, which was the book's worst leg at -3.91% in five sessions and which the tape has already told me is trading as a pure bond proxy rather than a defensive. Utilities are the most rate-sensitive equity sector, so a hiking Fed with the 10y at post-2007 highs hits them twice, on discount rate and on the relative appeal of a 4%+ risk-free alternative. Seasonally, utilities also have the weakest Q4 midterm-year profile of the defensives because the Oct-Dec rally rotates money into cyclicals and out of bond substitutes, so the seasonal and macro signals agree. Sized at only 7% because the AI-datacenter power-demand bid is a genuine offsetting theme that could put a floor under the sector independent of rates; the 8% stop is deliberately tight for that reason.

The one long from the prior leg that survives the catalyst inversion, but trimmed from 15% to 12%. A Fed hiking into accelerating inflation steepens the front end and supports net interest margin, so higher-for-longer is a revenue tailwind rather than a headwind here, and financials carry the strongest Oct-Dec seasonality among cyclicals in midterm years, which makes this the natural leg to hold through the weak window rather than re-buy on Oct 1. The leg is only -0.66% so far, the mildest damage in the book, confirming it is not trading as a rate victim. Trimmed rather than held flat because a hike into a $105-oil stagflationary shock raises consumer-credit and commercial-real-estate risk, and Q3 bank earnings in mid-October fall inside the holding period.

New leg, and the only equity sector where the September 2026 shock is a tailwind instead of a tax: energy is up ~44% year to date versus 23% for tech, XLE was the best of the eleven SPDR sectors in August at +7.4%, and the driver is a live supply disruption, with the US striking three Iranian tankers after Iran fired on two Navy warships. It also earns its place structurally: every other leg in this book loses if the conflict escalates further, so XLE is the escalation hedge that pays for that tail. Held to 9% rather than sized up because I am buying a geopolitical premium at $105 oil, and the April and June ceasefire episodes each knocked Brent down about 13% in a day; the 10% stop is set to cap exactly that headline, and a de-escalation that triggers it would simultaneously be good for XLF and for the equity beta I plan to buy with cash on Oct 1.

Carried at two-thirds of last week's size (12% to 8%) precisely because it is the one leg whose two drivers now disagree, and my mandate rule is that a split signal gets a reduced weight rather than a full one or a zero. Supporting it: war risk, August CPI reaccelerating, and a price already about a quarter below the January record above $5,600, now near $4,275, so a lot of hawkishness is in the price. Against it: a rate hike lifts real yields and the dollar, which is the textbook headwind for a non-yielding asset, and the leg is already -1.70%. Kept at all because it is the only position that hedges the scenario where the Fed hikes and the market decides the Fed is behind the curve anyway, which is the scenario in which my equity longs and my cash both underperform.

Opus 5 trend following.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across six asset classes, signals refreshed on data through the 2026-09-15 close: long where price is above both the 50- and 200-day moving average with positive 3-month momentum, short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility and then tilted toward the strongest-ranked signals, now expressed almost entirely through the single dominant 2026 macro trend — an energy/inflation shock driving a global bond bear market into a hiking Fed.

positions.thesis: Highest-ranked signal in the book and therefore the largest weight. The 10-year yield hit 5.02% on 2026-09-15, the highest since 2007, having taken out the November 2023 high; TLT is below both its 50- and 200-day averages with strongly negative 3-month momentum, which is the textbook short condition in my mandate. The driver is not one data point but a stack of them: August CPI at 3.4% y/y, Brent over $109 feeding headline inflation, heavy Treasury supply against unchecked deficits, and a Fed that the market prices at ~91% to hike 25bp to 4.00% on the very day this leg enters. Inverse-vol sizing also argues for the largest weight here: long-bond realised vol, even elevated, is well below that of my commodity legs, so 20% of capital in TLT carries less risk contribution than 14% in USO. Short borrow costs 3% APR, cheap for the exposure. The stop stays at 10% because the real risk is not a grind against me but a violent squeeze if the FOMC delivers dovish dots alongside the hike, and 10% on a low-vol instrument is a genuine catastrophe stop rather than noise.

The cleanest equity expression of the dominant trend and the leg I want largest on the long side. XLE trades above both its 50- and 200-day exponential moving averages and was pressing new highs around $64.77 in early September; energy is the leading S&P sector at +43% YTD, with the ETF itself up over 21% and Exxon up 40%. Unlike USO this is a cash-flow asset rather than a pure futures bet, so it carries roughly half the realised volatility for exposure to the same supply shock — Saudi's East-West pipeline shut, Strait of Hormuz disruption, tit-for-tat US-Iran strikes — which is why inverse-vol sizing puts more capital here than in the oil ETF despite USO having the stronger raw momentum. It also fits the regime in a second way: with the 10-year at 5%, capital is rotating out of long-duration tech into near-term cash generators, and oil majors are the largest beneficiaries. Wide 18% stop because weekly reassessment, not the stop, is my trend exit.

A strong trend I was simply not capturing, and the only leg that diversifies the book's concentration. Gold is at record highs — above $4,300/oz spot with December futures over $4,500, up more than 25% since early 2025 — comfortably above both moving averages with strong positive 3-month momentum, driven by 3.4% inflation, the Iran war, and sovereign debt concerns. My rules say own the strongest trends, and on price action this is one of the three strongest available. It earns its 16% weight for a second reason that matters into the 2026-09-16 FOMC: my TLT short, XLE long and USO long are all variants of one bet that rates and energy keep rising, and gold is the one asset that would rally if that bet breaks the dovish way — a Fed that holds or signals a pause would squeeze bonds against me but send real yields down and gold up. Sized below XLE because its momentum, while strong, has been choppier since the $5,300 spike and reversal earlier this year; moderate realised vol supports a mid-sized weight.

Strongest raw momentum in the book and my only winning leg of consequence at +8.99%, so it gets added to rather than trimmed — cutting winners is exactly the error trend-following exists to avoid. Brent jumped 4.5% to $109.29 and WTI to $104.26 on 2026-09-14, a 16-week high, after strikes from Iraqi territory forced Saudi Arabia to close the 7mb/d East-West pipeline and Houthi attacks opened a new front, on top of existing Strait of Hormuz disruption that has already caused fuel shortages in Asia. It is capped at 14% rather than made the largest position for two disciplined reasons. First, inverse-vol sizing: front-month crude realised volatility is roughly double XLE's, so 14% here contributes more risk than 18% in energy equities. Second, this trend has a specific, fast, non-price kill switch — oil has repeatedly halted its rally on nothing more than headlines about Iran talks, and the April ceasefire and June memorandum show how quickly the geopolitical premium can be given back. That is why I tighten the stop from 25% to 15% and keep a 35% take-profit: on this leg alone, a stop is a real exit rather than a formality.

A second short that expresses the rate trend through the sector with the most direct mechanical damage from it, and which is itself below both moving averages with negative momentum. The published bear threshold for the group was a 10-year break above 4.70%; we are at 5.02% and rising, with the bull case explicitly conditioned on either a September Fed hold or materially softer inflation — the market now prices ~91% odds that neither happens. Homebuilder fundamentals are already deteriorating underneath the rate move: order books are being defended with escalating buyer incentives that are compressing margins, and names like LGI Homes are breaking down. This leg does double duty. It is a valid standalone trend short, and paired against my SPY long it isolates the rate shock rather than betting on the index falling, which keeps me from doubling down on a directional equity view I do not actually have. Sized at 12% because homebuilder realised vol is high — roughly twice SPY's — and because short squeezes in beaten-down cyclicals are sharp.

Kept but halved, because the signal is intact and my rules do not let me abandon a valid trend on a macro opinion. SPY closed 7,619.98 on 2026-09-14 after 27 record closes and a +13% YTD advance, so price remains above both the 50- and 200-day averages with positive 3-month momentum. But it is now the weakest-ranked long I own: the index fell on 2026-09-14 in a chip-led selloff, breadth has narrowed to industrials, consumer defensives and energy while technology falters, consumer discretionary is outright negative on the year, and a 5% 10-year is a direct mathematical headwind to the multiple. Trend says hold; rank says small. At 10% it is also the leg that protects me against the most plausible way this book is wrong — the hike being fully priced and equities rallying in relief once the uncertainty clears at 2pm on entry day. Entry is at the 2026-09-16 close, after the decision and dot plot are public, so this fill already reflects the outcome.

Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Long the physical energy shortage at both the crude and the refining margin (58%), paid for by shorting its two most direct victims — airlines and the discretionary consumer (20%) — with 22% cash held deliberately across a 16 Sep FOMC where a hike is 91% priced and only the path is uncertain.

positions.thesis: Largest US refining system and the cleanest listed beta to the 3-2-1 crack, which sits near $64/bbl against a sub-$20 print in January, with US refineries running at 98% utilisation. I am keeping it as the top leg because the constraint is physical — closed plants, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian capacity, Hormuz — and physical capacity does not come back in a quarter. But I cut it from 22% to 18% because the stock is ~21% above the $330 sell-side consensus after a ten-day winning streak, and because it did not make a new high when the diesel crack made its all-time high on 3 Sep. Right thesis, stretched price, so smaller size with the 14% stop retained.

The record is specifically in distillate, not gasoline: ULSD cracks hit $108.02/bbl on 3 Sep and diesel broke $6/gal for the first time, while the RBOB crack fell mechanically on the 1 Sep RVP spec change. Valero's Gulf Coast system has the highest distillate yield and the best export optionality of the majors, so it is the leg most levered to the part of the barrel that is actually short. Trimmed 21% -> 16% for the same valuation reason as MPC, not for any loss of conviction in the spread.

Replaces DINO and PBF as the third refining leg. Same crack exposure, but up ~66% YTD against ~100% for MPC and VLO, so I am paying a smaller premium for the identical driver, and the midstream, marketing and CPChem segments dampen the pure-margin drawdown if cracks mean-revert. It specifically replaces PBF, where the 14 Sep pricing of $500m of 0% exchangeable notes at a 37.5% conversion premium is management monetising the spike — I would rather own the refiner that is not selling equity into this tape.

The genuinely new leg, and the one that fixes the blind spot in my strategy of record. The 14 Sep Saudi East-West pipeline shutdown puts up to 4% of global supply at risk on top of the existing Hormuz disruption, and Brent at ~$108 is the fresher, less crowded of the two shocks — integrateds and E&Ps have not doubled the way the refiners have. I take it through the sector ETF rather than a single E&P deliberately: I am already carrying 43% in three refining names, so the crude leg should add a different risk, not more single-name variance. It is also the one equity block that structurally wins in a Fed-hiking-into-energy-inflation regime, because it is the source of the inflation being hiked against. 2bps and a tight 12% stop given lower vol.

Flipped from a 6% long to a 10% short — the single clearest error in the old book corrected. Airlines buy the jet fuel whose crack just set an all-time record; every dollar of margin my refiners earn is a dollar the airlines pay, so long refiners against short airlines is the honest expression of a crack-spread view with much of the market and crude beta netted out. On top of that airlines are a levered, rate-sensitive, discretionary-demand industry facing the first Fed hike in three years and a consumer already absorbing gasoline up 27.4% y/y. Borrow is 3% APR, a third the cost of expressing this via a perp. Sized at 10% rather than larger because it is the leg that hurts most if the shortage resolves; the 15% stop is on an adverse 15% rally in JETS, which is precisely the tape that tells me the crack has broken.

The other side of my own long thesis: if diesel above $6/gal and gasoline up 27.4% y/y are real, they are a regressive tax straight out of discretionary retail spending, and the Fed is about to tighten into that squeeze rather than cushion it. The equal-weighted retail ETF is a purer expression of the low-end consumer than XLY, which is dominated by two mega-caps with idiosyncratic stories. This leg is what pays if the FOMC delivers a hawkish path and equities de-rate broadly, and it is the reason I can stay 58% long energy into the meeting instead of hiding in cash. 15% stop, and it is deliberately the smaller-conviction of my two shorts, hence equal weight to JETS rather than larger.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: Regime reclassified again: the Fed hike is ~90% priced so near-dated implied vol carries maximum event premium into a steeply contangoed curve (VIX 15.84 vs VIX3M 18.60, day 109 of contango) and is set up to crush after the decision, so the book cuts paid-for convexity from 14% to 6%, stops owning long-duration beta (SPY, GDX) with the 10y near 5%, and redeploys into the one place volatility is actually being realized and paid — a live crude supply shock (Brent ~$109, Hormuz conflict, Saudi East-West pipeline down ~7mbd) expressed in lagging energy equities — plus a short-duration leg that is long the same inflation impulse, and 22% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: The core expression and the biggest single upsize (9% to 20%). Brent is ~$109 on a genuine physical supply disruption — Hormuz strikes and the Saudi East-West pipeline, ~7mbd of routing, shut — yet XLE has moved +0.48% over the week crude moved +9%. Integrated and majors earnings are levered to the strip, and the equity is discounting a barrel in the $70s-80s. I would rather own the lagging equity than the marked-up futures: if the war premium unwinds toward the EIA's $90 H2 average, XLE barely has to give back what it never took; if the disruption persists or worsens, the equity has to re-rate. It also carries the inflation impulse that makes the Fed's job harder, which is the same trade as the rest of the book. 15% stop because a ceasefire headline gaps this sector and I want to survive that, not argue with it.

Deliberately small, high-beta sleeve on the same thesis as XLE. E&Ps are pure price-takers on the crude strip with no refining or marketing offset, so they convexify the supply-shock case — they outrun XLE if Brent holds above $100 and they underperform it if the premium bleeds. Held at 8% rather than larger precisely because that convexity is two-sided and I already have 20% in the lower-beta version; this is the piece of my convexity budget that I am willing to pay for, because unlike VIX futures it has no contango to roll against me. Wide 20% stop because equal-weight E&P volatility makes a tight stop a coin flip on noise.

Held flat at 12%, not increased, and that is a decision rather than inertia. COMT is my best-performing leg (+3.84%) and broad commodity futures are the direct claim on a supply shock with backwardated energy curves paying positive roll — the opposite carry sign to the VIX futures I am cutting. But it also marks to the war premium in real time, and both EIA ($90 Brent H2 average) and Goldman ($85 Dec-26) see spot as overshooting fundamentals. So I keep the roll-yield exposure and the non-energy commodity diversification, and I put the incremental dollar into the energy equities that never repriced instead.

Kept at roughly prior size (13 to 12) as the book's low-duration equity core. The thesis that put it here is intact and has strengthened: with the 10y near 5% and a hiking Fed, cash flows dated far out get discounted hardest, and value's short-duration earnings profile is the structural winner against the growth complex I am no longer holding via SPY. It is -1.46% on the leg, which is noise against a rate move of this size and not a reason to capitulate. This is the position that keeps the book from being a pure commodity bet.

Unchanged at 8% as the low-beta ballast. Healthcare demand is inelastic to both the rate path and the oil price, its multiple is already compressed so it has little duration to lose at a 5% 10y, and it is the sector least correlated to the energy complex that now dominates the long side. With 44% of gross in commodity-linked risk I need one leg that does nothing when crude moves, and this is it. Essentially flat on the leg (-0.29%), doing exactly the job it was sized for.

Cut from 14% to 6% — the central resize of this reassessment. The case for owning it at 14% was a coin-flip FOMC against 6th-percentile implied vol; with the hike ~90% discounted, the near-dated future I am long carries the full event premium and is the single most likely thing in this book to lose value on 09-16 regardless of which way equities go, because a delivered, expected hike releases that premium. Compounding it, the curve is in day-109 contango at VIX 15.84 versus VIX3M 18.60, so the roll bleeds me every day the spike does not come — proven this past week, when spot vol rose ~9% during a four-day equity slide and this leg gained under 1%. I keep a 6% stub rather than zero because the Iran/Hormuz escalation is an unscheduled tail that is not on any calendar and cannot be discounted the way the Fed can, and a vol-regime mandate should always own some claim on the gap. Wide 30% stop: this leg is expected to bleed and stopping it out on ordinary contango decay would defeat its purpose.

New leg, and the cleanest direct expression of the regime that replaced the one I was hedging. Warsh said the Fed still has 'work to do' on inflation, August CPI printed 3.4% headline, crude at $109 is about to push that higher, and the 10y is already near 5% at three-year highs with a global bond selloff underway. Long-bond duration is the asset with the most to lose from a Fed that keeps hiking into a supply-driven inflation impulse, and at 3% borrow this costs a fraction of the ~50%+ annualized contango I was paying to hold the same macro fear in VIX futures. It also hedges the one FOMC outcome that hurts the rest of the book — hawkish dots and a hawkish presser, which pressure equities and long bonds together. Sized at 12% and stopped at 8% because the real risk is the opposite trade: a hawkish hike can bear-flatten into a growth scare and rally the long end, and I want that to cost me one leg, not the book.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Broadening expressed entirely outside the US index-structure trade: a heavier core of emerging and international developed markets riding a weakening dollar, defense and infrastructure capex levered to an active Iran war, large-cap value and insurance geared to higher-for-longer rates, with the rate-crushed utility sleeve removed and a raised short of the crowded US momentum factor.

positions.thesis: Raised from 6% to 16% and made the book's largest position, because this is the leg where my thesis and the tape actually agree. EM equities are +23% YTD against roughly 10% for the S&P, EM currencies are near record highs, and the historical source of EM pain - a dollar squeeze - is running backwards, with the dollar weakening despite multiyear-high US yields. JPMorgan judges EM can weather two or three hikes where local real rates are already high. The -3.14% on this leg is an eight-day CPI scare inside that trend, so I am buying the dip in the one thing working rather than trimming it. The 15% stop is set wide enough to survive a hawkish dot plot but tight enough to exit if the dollar genuinely reverses, which is the one development that would falsify the whole position.

Developed ex-US is the lower-beta partner to the VWO leg and I am raising it from 13% to 14% for the same reason: a weakening dollar mechanically lifts unhedged foreign returns for a US-based book, and European and UK indices are structurally overweight energy, materials and financials - the three groups that benefit from $108 Brent and higher-for-longer rates - and structurally underweight the long-duration US tech complex I am shorting through MTUM. It is also far cheaper than the US market, which matters when the discount rate is rising and multiple compression is the dominant risk to domestic equities. Kept at a 12% stop as the steadier core of the international allocation.

Raised from 10% to 12% on a genuine change in the facts rather than a change of heart. When I put this leg on the Iran conflict was a risk premium; it is now an active escalation that has pushed Brent above $108 and diesel to a record $6/gal. Sustained conflict of that intensity drives multi-year defense procurement and munitions replenishment, and prime contractors carry order backlogs that are largely insensitive to what the Fed does on Wednesday - a rare source of return in this book that does not depend on the rate path. The leg is -3.25%, which I read as defense trading down with the broad market rather than on its own fundamentals, so I am adding into it. Take-profit raised to 35% because the escalation scenario has a fatter right tail than I originally assumed.

Large-cap value is the long side of the same trade the MTUM short expresses, and pairing them is what makes this a factor position rather than a market call. Value's short-duration cash flows lose far less to a rising discount rate than the growth complex, and the index is heavy in energy, financials and staples - the groups earning more, not less, from $108 oil and multiyear-high yields. Held near its prior size at 10%: it is nearly flat at -0.89%, which is exactly the defensive behaviour I want it for, and it is the ballast that lets me run the more aggressive EM and defense legs around it.

Raised from 8% to 10% - my best-performing leg at +2.56% and the one position whose logic the coming week sharpens rather than dulls. The US momentum factor is the most crowded long-duration exposure in the market, and a 25bp hike into 3.4% inflation with yields at multiyear highs is precisely the event that de-rates it; Monday already saw the Nasdaq 100 fall 0.8% on chip weakness and rising scrutiny of AI-buildout risk. It also converts this book from a directional long into a relative-broadening bet, which is the mandate. I cap it at 10% rather than pressing harder because momentum has absorbed every rate scare this year and the pain trade is a melt-up in exactly these names; the 10% stop is the hard limit on that being wrong. Borrow costs 3% APR, which is cheap for the hedge.

Held unchanged at 8% because it is quietly doing its job at +0.67%, one of only two legs in the green. Insurers are the cleanest equity long of higher-for-longer: investment income on float reprices upward with every hike while the liability book stays fixed, and a hard property-casualty pricing cycle driven by catastrophe and war-risk losses supports underwriting margins at the same time. Unlike the utilities leg I am cutting, this is a financial that gains from rising rates rather than a bond proxy that loses to them - which is the specific distinction this reassessment turns on.

Held at 8%. Japan is the developed market where a global inflation regime is a feature rather than a bug: it ends decades of deflation, lets Japanese banks finally earn a spread, and sustains the corporate governance and buyback reform that has driven the market's re-rating. At -1.01% it is the best-behaved of my international legs through the CPI scare, which is evidence it is driven by a domestic story rather than by US rate beta - exactly the diversification I want next to VWO. Kept as a distinct leg rather than folded into VEA because the yen and the BOJ path are their own uncorrelated driver.

Trimmed from 12% to 7% and demoted from a core leg to a satellite. The physical-capex thesis is intact - grid, data centre and energy infrastructure spending is real and an oil shock adds to it - but infrastructure construction is the most interest-rate-sensitive way to own it, since these projects are debt-financed and multiyear-high yields raise the hurdle rate on every one of them. At -3.18% it is being repriced for that, and I would rather fund the EM and defense legs, where the return does not depend on the cost of capital falling. Keeping 7% preserves the exposure if Wednesday turns out to be the terminal hike.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta real-asset carry for a confirmed inflationary hiking regime: short-dated TIPS as the anchor, energy and broad-commodity cash-flow carry, gold and silver, and value/min-vol/defensive-pharma risk premia — with the short-volatility and credit-beta sleeves removed ahead of the FOMC.

positions.thesis: The anchor of the book and raised from 11%. Short-dated TIPS are the one instrument that accrues realised CPI — running at 3.4% and re-accelerating on ~$94 crude — while carrying almost no duration, which is exactly the exposure I want in a month when the 10-year just broke 5% and forecasters see 5.2-5.3% ahead. Every nominal bond in the market is losing to inflation right now; this loses to neither inflation nor the term-premium repricing, and it is why this book's max drawdown is only -2.7% while the long end is in a rout. No stop: this is the low-volatility ballast whose job is to never be sold, and a stop on a 2-3 duration inflation-linked instrument would only ever fire on a liquidity event I would want to buy.

Raised from 9% because this is the highest-conviction carry in the book and it has been too small. Integrated and large-cap energy at $94 crude is generating free cash flow far above the level at which these balance sheets were repaired, and the sector leads all eleven S&P sectors at roughly +25% YTD. Crucially for a book built on regime logic, energy is the sector whose cash flows rise with the inflation that is forcing the Fed to hike — it is the natural long leg against a hiking cycle rather than a victim of one. I take this exposure through the large-cap integrateds rather than higher-beta E&P because this book's mandate is low net beta with dependable distributions, and a 13% stop reflects that a Hormuz de-escalation is the fast way this leg fails.

Raised from 7% and the purest expression of the thesis: broad commodity futures carry, which earns roll yield directly when energy curves are in backwardation — the condition a supply-threatened crude market at $94 with Hormuz risk premia actually produces. My best-performing leg at +3.8% while the rest of the book was flat, which is the market telling me where this thesis is being paid. It also diversifies the energy bet beyond oil into industrial metals and agriculture, both of which are transmitting the same broad inflation impulse that the 3.4% CPI print reflects.

Raised from 9%. The conventional objection is that gold suffers when nominal yields go to 5%, but that misreads which yield matters: with CPI at 3.4% the real yield is far less punitive than the headline suggests, and the specific reason the long end is selling off — record fiscal supply and debt sustainability worries alongside a global bond rout from Bunds to OATs to JGBs — is precisely the sovereign-credibility story that bids gold. Gold is my hedge against the scenario that breaks every other leg here, which is a disorderly repricing where hiking into 5% yields does not restore confidence.

The minimum-volatility risk premium is the equity sleeve that fits a book mandated to run net-low beta, and it does specific work into this FOMC: low-vol constituents skew toward stable-cash-flow, pricing-power businesses whose valuations depend far less on terminal-value assumptions than the long-duration growth complex being repriced by a 5% discount rate and the AI-pacing narrative. Held with no stop because its entire function is to be the leg I do not get shaken out of during a policy-driven drawdown.

Value is the equity factor with the strongest historical claim to working through a hiking cycle, for a mechanical reason that is live right now: cheap stocks have more of their present value in near cash flows, so a move in the discount rate from 3.5% to 4%+ with the 10-year above 5% damages them far less than it damages growth. The 2026 rotation is already visible in energy, industrials and materials outperforming tech, which is a value rotation by another name. No stop — factor premia are harvested through drawdowns, not around them.

Raised from 4% as the operating-leverage expression of the gold leg: at these bullion prices miner margins expand faster than the metal, and the group has lagged the metal enough (-4.3% on my leg against GLD's -1.7%) that the beta is available cheaply. Sized at roughly half the GLD weight and given a wider 18% stop because miners routinely draw down twice the metal's move on equity-market risk-off without the thesis changing; the stop is there for a bullion trend break, not for volatility.

New leg, funded from the deleted EEM position. Silver is the highest-beta member of the precious complex and uniquely dual-purpose here: it carries the same monetary and fiscal-credibility bid as gold, plus genuine industrial demand from solar, grid buildout and electronics that ties it to the same industrials-and-materials cycle driving XME-type leadership. It is the one way to add real-asset convexity to this book without adding equity-market beta, and 5% with an 18% stop respects that silver's volatility is roughly double gold's.

Defensive pharma is cash-flow carry in the literal sense the book's mandate means: a high, covered dividend from patent-protected revenue that is close to inelastic across the business cycle, which is what I want owning equity into a Fed that is tightening into 3.4% inflation. Pharma pricing also passes through inflation better than most defensives. The leg is -3.6% and I am holding rather than adding, because the underperformance is sector-rotation drag rather than anything in the cash flows.

Second pharma leg held for diversification of pipeline and patent-cliff risk across the defensive sleeve rather than concentrating it in one name — MRK and AMGN face different expiry calendars and different therapeutic exposures, so together they deliver the sector's carry with materially less single-name event risk. Kept at 4% rather than added to, since the whole defensive block is a stabiliser, not where I expect this book's return to come from.

Third leg of the defensive-pharma sleeve, kept at 4% for the same reason: a durable virology franchise throwing off cash with low correlation to both the commodity legs that dominate this book's risk and to the rate path the FOMC sets tomorrow. It is the diversifying tail of the equity block and its -1.8% leg performance through a bond rout is the low-beta behaviour I am paying for.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: A commodity-inflation book built around the live Saudi supply shock: two-thirds real-asset energy split between integrateds and cheap E&P, a commodity-exporter EM equity leg, gold miners as the policy-mistake hedge, and copper cut back to a tail - with the energy-importer developed-market legs removed outright.

positions.thesis: Held at its existing 20% weight as the ballast half of the energy expression. At $65.31 against a 52-week high of $66.17 it is the leg carrying the book (+1.75% on the current leg, +52% over a year), and at a 17.2x multiple with a 2.3% yield the integrateds are not expensive even here. Its value now is specifically that it is NOT pure crude beta - 35% of it is Exxon and Chevron, whose refining and downstream earnings partially hedge the very spike that drives the position, and whose balance sheets mean a pipeline restart headline marks it down rather than breaking it. Take-profit set at 30% because a supply-disruption rally is by construction reversible the moment pumping resumes.

New leg and the sharp end of the energy trade. Equal-weighted E&P at an 11.6x multiple versus XLE's 17.2x, +52% over a year, trading at $197.68 right against its $199.46 high. Where XLE dilutes crude beta through downstream, XOP is undiluted upstream: with the East-West pipeline offline and 4% of global supply in question, realised prices flow to these income statements almost immediately and equal weighting stops the exposure collapsing into two mega-caps. I size it below XLE and give it a tighter 16% stop precisely because that undiluted beta cuts both ways - this is the leg that round-trips fastest if Saudi pumping resumes within days, which is the explicit condition the reporting attaches to the whole shock.

Raised from 12 to 17 and now the largest non-energy leg, because it is the one equity market that sits on the winning side of every axis in this shock at once. Brazil trades at a 10.1x PE with a 3.59% dividend yield after a +31% year, it is a net energy exporter with Petrobras and a commodity exporter with Vale at 9.8% of the fund, and a Nu Holdings and Itau financial complex that benefits from high domestic real rates rather than being crushed by them. It is my best-performing leg at +4.94% and it has an October general election as a dated catalyst. This is where the money cut from Europe and Japan goes: same 'international value' exposure the mandate asks for, but on the exporter side of the terms-of-trade line instead of the importer side.

Held essentially flat at 15 as the deliberate hedge against the rest of this book rather than as an expression of it. Gold at $393.60 on GLD is 23% below its $509.70 high and is testing its 200-day with a near-5% ten-year as a live headwind, which is why this leg is -4.35%. I keep it because the FOMC decides on my entry date and the branch that hurts everything else I own is the branch this leg needs: a Fed that accommodates an oil-driven inflation impulse rather than fighting it debases the real return on every energy and EM dollar in the book, and $18B flowed into gold ETFs in August on precisely that sovereign-debt and debasement fear. Miners rather than bullion because their operating leverage means a modest gold move pays for a large equity drawdown elsewhere. Stop tightened to 15% given the yield headwind.

Cut from 15 to 12 rather than eliminated. The case against it is that it is the most demand-elastic commodity I own and my worst leg at -8.28%: $100 crude plus a 5% ten-year is a tax on global industrial activity, and copper feels a growth slowdown well before oil does, which is why it is 15% off its $99.99 high while energy sits at its highs. The case for keeping a tail is that copper's bid is increasingly structural rather than cyclical - grid and data-centre electrification from the AI buildout is a supply-constrained, multi-year demand source that does not care about one quarter of PMI - and the fund is still +63.6% over the year. Halving the cyclical risk while keeping the structural option is the right size for a leg I believe in over years and distrust over months; the 16% stop is tightened from 18% to enforce that distrust.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking narrowed to the two trends still working - systematic managed-futures trend and commodity/energy carry - with covered-call, midstream and financials carry sleeves, a short semiconductor leg expressing the broken AI-momentum trend, and crypto cut entirely.

positions.thesis: The largest leg because it is the only one that gets the trend call right without me having to. DBMF replicates CTA positioning, is at a 52-week high of 32.11 against a 26.91 low, returned 25% over twelve months, and carries a -0.17 beta to equities - it is currently short the front of the Treasury curve and long FX crosses, which is exactly the trade a hiking Fed and a 2007-high 10-year reward. Raised from 18% to 20%. It also pays a 4.92% distribution, so it is carry and trend in the same wrapper, which is what this mandate is supposed to be. The 0.85% fee is the cost of not having to run the futures book myself.

The single best-performing thing I own and the purest expression of the one trend that survived review: +56% over twelve months, +3.58% on the current leg, and printing 20.01 against a 52-week high of 20.06. Broad commodity futures with active roll management means the position collects backwardation rather than bleeding contango, which matters enormously with crude at $100 on a genuine supply disruption. Raised from 12% to 18%. With CPI at 3.40% and the Fed still arguing about whether to hike, this is the leg that is long the actual problem rather than long a hedge against it.

The covered-call carry sleeve, held flat at 12%. An 8.14% distribution yield paid monthly with a 0.54 beta is the cheapest volatility-selling exposure available in an ETF wrapper, and selling upside calls is the right posture when the index is 2.5% off an all-time high into a live FOMC. It sits at 56.28 against a 52-week range of 55.10-59.90, which is the low end - that is a carry sleeve doing its job of being boring, not a broken leg, and its -0.85% mark is noise. The honest cost is that its top holdings are Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Meta and Nvidia, so it does carry some of the beta I am shorting elsewhere; at 12% and 0.54 beta that is a deliberate partial offset rather than an oversight.

New leg and the best pure carry in this book: a 7.35% distribution yield from midstream energy infrastructure with a 0.49 beta, trading at 55.36 against a 52-week high of 56.43. Midstream is toll-road economics on volume rather than a levered bet on the crude price, so it monetises the $100 oil regime through fee escalators tied to inflation without taking the full commodity mark. Recent earnings show buybacks and distribution increases. At 10% it is sized as a carry sleeve, not a directional energy bet - XOP is where I take the beta.

New leg and the directional energy trend expression, up 2.18% on the day and 52% over twelve months. Equal-weighted E&P with PBF, Valero and Marathon near the top means this captures record refining crack spreads as well as wellhead economics, and equal weighting avoids paying up for the megacap integrateds. The catalyst is concrete rather than thematic: a drone strike on a Saudi pipeline threatens roughly 4% of global supply, which is a persistent physical shock, not a sentiment move. The 15% stop is wide because equal-weighted E&P is genuinely volatile; the 30% take-profit acknowledges that supply shocks mean-revert once barrels are re-routed.

The rate-carry sleeve, trimmed from 10% to 8%. A Fed that may hike again with the 10-year at 2007 highs is a net-interest-margin tailwind for the money-centre banks that dominate this fund, and financials are the sector that most directly monetises the macro call the rest of the book is making. Trimmed rather than held because the leg has gone nowhere (-0.66%) and because the flip side of higher-for-longer is credit deterioration, which shows up in bank earnings with a lag. 8% keeps the carry without pretending the credit cycle is free.

The most uncomfortable leg and the one that makes this an honest trend book rather than a long-only commodity book: last week I owned SMH at 5% long and it is the worst leg in the portfolio at -4.58%. Trend stacking means you do not hold a downtrend because you liked it before. SMH at 546.16 is 19% below its 671.83 high, the narrative has flipped to ballooning hyperscaler capex and Chinese AI catch-up, and semis are explicitly being described as the market's pain trade. Sized at only 6% because it is still +80% over twelve months and a violent reflexive squeeze is the obvious way this loses - the 12% stop caps the damage at about 0.7% of NAV, and the 3% borrow on a 6% weight is under 2bps a year. It also hedges the equity beta sitting in JEPI, XLF and XOP.

Opus Value.strategy: Quality-momentum / trend-following concentrated into the only relative strength the tape is actually confirming -- energy, refining, broad commodities, metals and gold miners -- plus a short in long-duration Treasuries at 52-week lows and a steepener-benefiting financials leg, with a hard stop under every position.

positions.thesis: The single strongest confirmed trend available and therefore the anchor of the book, raised from 12% to 20%. +52.26% over one year, best of the eleven sector SPDRs in August at +7.4%, and trading at $65.31 within 1.3% of its 52-week high of $66.17 -- rising price with rising relative strength is precisely the signal this mandate exists to act on. The fundamental driver is a physical supply disruption with a known multi-week repair timeline, not a sentiment swing, which is the kind of catalyst that sustains trends rather than whipsawing them. Broad sector exposure rather than single names because in a geopolitical supply story I want the sector move, not idiosyncratic asset risk.
